parts.goal: Learn how a problem can solve itself by breaking into smaller versions.

sections.title: Recursion Idea
sections.body:
Imagine climbing stairs.

To reach stair 10, you first reach stair 9.
To reach stair 9, you first reach stair 8.

Large problems become smaller until they are easy.
This is recursion.

sections.title: Base Case
sections.body:
Every recursive solution needs a stopping point.

Without a stopping point, it never ends.

This stopping point is called the Base Case.

Exercise:
Give three real-life examples where a task naturally stops.

sections.title: Recursive Thinking
sections.body:
Examples:
- Opening nested boxes.
- Looking through folders.
- Family tree.

Each step is similar to the previous one.

sections.title: Compare With Loops
sections.body:
Loops repeat.

Recursion calls itself.

Some problems are easier with loops.
Others are easier with recursion.

Exercise:
Compare washing dishes using a loop and recursion.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
Mistakes:
- No base case.
- Wrong recursive call.
- Infinite recursion.

Always ask:
'When does this stop?'

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Practice:
1. Count down from 10.
2. Count up to 20.
3. Describe nested folders.
4. Explain recursion using Russian dolls.
5. Explain recursion using mirrors.

sections.title: Mini Project
sections.body:

Design a Folder Explorer.

Each folder may contain:
- Files

quiz: Why is the base case important?

sections.title: Why Sorting
sections.body:
Sorting puts information into order.
Examples: books on a shelf, students by height, scores from highest to lowest.
Exercise: List 10 things that can be sorted.

sections.title: Bubble Sort
sections.body:
Bubble Sort compares neighboring items and swaps them until everything is ordered.
Real-life example: moving the tallest person step by step to the end of a line.
Practice: Sort numbers 5,2,4,1,3 manually.

sections.title: Selection Sort
sections.body:
Selection Sort finds the smallest item and places it first.
Example: choosing the smallest card from your hand.
Exercise: Sort 8,3,6,1,5.

sections.title: Insertion Sort
sections.body:
Insertion Sort inserts each new item into the correct position.
Example: placing playing cards into your hand.
Exercise: Explain how you sort exam papers.

sections.title: Merge Quick
sections.body:
Merge Sort splits a problem into smaller parts and merges them.
Quick Sort chooses a pivot and partitions values.
You don't need the code yet—understand the idea first.

sections.title: Comparison
sections.body:
Bubble: simple, slow.
Selection: simple, fewer swaps.
Insertion: good for small nearly-sorted lists.
Merge & Quick: much faster for large data.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Practice:
1. Sort student names.
2. Sort prices.
3. Sort dates.
4. Explain which algorithm you'd choose and why.

sections.title: Mini Project
sections.body: Mini Project: Design a scoreboard that always keeps players sorted from highest score to lowest.

quiz: Which algorithms are generally faster on large data?

parts.goal: Understand how large software systems are organized.

sections.title: What Is Architecture
sections.body:
Architecture is the blueprint of a software system.
Like a house needs rooms, software needs organized parts.
Exercise: Draw the rooms of your house and explain their jobs.

sections.title: Client Server
sections.body:
Client asks, Server answers.
Example: Your phone requests weather data, the server sends it back.
Exercise: Describe ordering food using the client-server idea.

sections.title: Frontend Backend
sections.body:
Frontend is what users see.
Backend processes data and business logic.
Database stores information.
Exercise: Identify these parts in a social media app.

sections.title: Modules
sections.body:
Large projects are split into modules.
Examples: Auth, Chat, Payments, Notifications.
Each module has one responsibility.

sections.title: APIs
sections.body:
An API is a bridge between systems.
Example: A waiter carries your order to the kitchen and brings food back.
Exercise: Think of three real-life 'API' examples.

sections.title: Scalability
sections.body:
Good architecture allows growth.
Start small, then improve as users increase.
Avoid making everything one huge file.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Practice:
Design the architecture of:
- Notes App
- Online Shop
- School System
List frontend, backend, database and APIs.

sections.title: Mini Project
sections.body:
Mini Project:
Design the architecture of a simple social network.
Include login, posts, chat, notifications and database.

parts.goal: Learn how information is stored and organized.

sections.title: What Is Database
sections.body:
A database is an organized collection of information.
Examples: school records, hospital patients, online shop products.
Exercise: List five places where databases are used.

sections.title: Tables Rows Columns
sections.body:
A table stores one type of information.
Columns describe attributes.
Rows represent records.
Exercise: Draw a Student table with Name, Age and Grade.

sections.title: Primary Foreign Keys
sections.body:
Primary Key uniquely identifies a row.
Foreign Key connects two tables.
Real-life example: Student ID links students to exam results.
Exercise: Design two related tables.

sections.title: Relationships
sections.body:
Relationships:
One-to-One
One-to-Many
Many-to-Many
Exercise: Explain relationships using teachers, students and classes.

sections.title: SQL Basics
sections.body:
Basic SQL ideas:
SELECT
INSERT
UPDATE
DELETE
No need to memorize syntax yet—understand what each command does.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.body:
Common mistakes:
Duplicate records
Missing IDs
Wrong relationships
Poor table design
Exercise: Explain why duplicate student IDs are a problem.

sections.title: Practice
sections.body:
Practice:
Design databases for:
- Library
- Hospital
- Online Shop
- Football Team
List tables and relationships.

sections.title: Mini Project
sections.body:
Mini Project:
Design a database for a social media app.
Include Users, Posts, Comments, Likes and Followers.
Explain how the tables connect.

parts.goal: Learn how large applications are designed to serve many users reliably.

sections.title: What Is System Design
sections.body:
System Design is planning how all parts of a software system work together.

Think of designing a city:
- Roads
- Buildings
- Water
- Electricity

Software also needs planning before building.

sections.title: Monolith vs Microservices
sections.body:
Monolith:
Everything is in one application.

Microservices:
Many smaller services work together.

Exercise:
List advantages of each approach.

sections.title: Scalability
sections.body:
Scalability means handling more users without major problems.

Ways to scale:
- Bigger servers (vertical)
- More servers (horizontal)

Exercise:
Explain how a restaurant serves more customers.

sections.title: Load Balancer
sections.body:
A Load Balancer distributes requests across multiple servers.

Analogy:
A traffic officer directing cars to different roads.

Exercise:
Describe another real-life example.

sections.title: Cache and Queue
sections.body:
Cache stores frequently used data.
Message Queues allow systems to process work step by step.

Examples:
- Notifications
- Email sending
- Image processing

sections.title: High Availability
sections.body:
High Availability keeps services running even if one server fails.

Fault Tolerance allows the system to continue working despite failures.

Exercise:
Think of backup generators in a hospital.
